Beállítom Vályi-Nagy Vilmos, a második Orbán-kormány infokommunikációért felelős államtitkára arról beszélt a Partizánnak adott interjújában, hogy Pintér Sándor egykori belügyminiszter 2014-től kezdve több mint két éven keresztül folyamatosan megfigyeltette. Szerinte emögött az lehetett, hogy Pintér félt, hogy információi lehetnek az úgynevezett Eclipse-ügyben. Ez volt a kétezres évek egyik legnagyobb korrupciós botránya, és Pintér Sándor is érintett volt: lánya az autók eredetiségvizsgálatának informatikai rendszereit kialakító és üzemeltető Eclipse-nél volt projektmenedzser, a vállalkozás Pintér korábbi cégétől, a Civil Biztonsági Szolgálat (CBSZ) Zrt.-től bérelt irodákat az Angol utcában, egy magas rangú rendőr pedig az Eclipse német rendszámú Mercedesét használta. Vályi-Nagy állítása szerint Pintér többször megpróbálta elérni Orbánnál a leváltását. Közben fenyegetéseket kapott, megüzenték neki, hogy költözzen el az országból. 2014 nyarán tartott egy búcsúebédet azoknak a kollégáinak, akikkel jóban volt, ezt is teljes egészében rögzítette a szakszolgálat. „Ott ültek az Alkotmányvédelmi Hivatal munkatársai, mint egy árnyék, követtek mindenhová” – mondta a volt államtitkár. Szerinte Pintér miatt nem kapott lehetőséget 2014-ben a kormányban. Vályi-Nagy azt mondta, hogy a megfigyelésnek 2016-ban lett vége, bár később is volt ilyesmire példa, legutóbb például tavaly nyáron. Ilyen esetekben mindig szóltak neki előre az ismerősei, ami szerinte mutatta, hogy mennyire nem működött a rendszer az elmúlt években. Deutsche Bank shares plunged on Tuesday after the publication of damning internal documents Image: Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP Advertisement Deutsche Bank is in damage control mode again after an international consortium of more than 200 investigative journalists published internal documents from the global lender on Tuesday under the name "Inside Deutsche Bank." The documents, published in Der Spiegel, Financial Times, Le Monde and The New York Times, among others, cover Deutsche Bank 's business dealings with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein , now US President Donald Trump , and a host of Russian oligarchs. Gleaned from nearly 15 million documents leaked to a journalist from India and another from South Africa, the e-mails and meeting minutes trace the bank's aggressive pursuit of business deals in Russia, and with high-profile Russian oligarchs, right up until Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — despite risk warnings from numerous managers. Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing was among the executives who took part in the bank's Russia strategy working group. The bank also still employs more than 160 people in Russia and generated 2025 pre-tax profits of €61 million ($67 million) there through a local subsidiary. Money laundering, oligarchs, terrorists: How corrupt are the banks? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Not just about Deutsche Bank's business with Trump, Epstein and Russians In all, the documents cover the past 20 years of the German lender's business dealings and raise questions about the efficacy of internal controls by showing that Deutsche Bank had repeatedly put financial interests before international sanctions compliance and anti-money laundering rules. Other red flags raised in Tuesday's reports suggest that Deutsche Bank sought to set up tax-optimization schemes for wealthy clients, that criminal networks may have been able to move illicit cash through the institution, that it helped facilitate arms deals, that it helped companies in environmentally damaging industries and that it held funds for the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party. Has Deutsche Bank really changed its ways? Beyond more recent negative headlines involving alleged anti-money laundering and compliance failures, Deutsche Bank has been trying to restore its public image ever since its involvement in the US subprime mortgage rate scandal helped trigger the 2008 global financial crisis — a fiasco that ultimately cost the bank more than €20 billion in penalties and settlements. When Sewing later took over in 2018, he promised to turn the institution around . Although he has made Deutsche Bank profitable once again, he did so at the cost of massive job cuts , and some compliance failings have continued. Sewing to the German business daily Handelsblatt that some mistakes had been made under his leadership. "When you look at the events today, you naturally ask yourself whether you could have done some things differently," he told the paper. "I am not without mistakes," he said, but added that the course he set for the bank "has always been right and remains so." The bank's shares fell by up to 6% in Tuesday trading. German government wants 'full transparency' from Deutsche Bank Deutsche Bank issued a statement claiming that the reports were old news and that the institution had long ago turned over a new leaf. In an e-mailed statement to the press, Deutsche Bank Supervisory Board Chairman Alexander Wynaendts wrote, "During my tenure I haven't seen a single decision from Christian Sewing that I was not comfortable with." A Tuesday statement from the bank described the revelations as "legacy" matters and claimed they would have no lasting negative financial impact on the institution. Nevertheless, German Finance Minister and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil on Tuesday called on Deutsche Bank to "provide full transparency regarding how it has addressed past failures and internal control deficiencies and how it will effectively prevent these in the future." Further, Klingbeil said authorities must investigate and "take necessary action" where appropriate.
